Meanwhile, P/E ratios have not changed very significantly. This means that to sustain the trend in both stock price and P/E, company earnings must increase YOY by more than inflation.

 More and more money is created. Yet that new money is unevenly distributed, with much more of it going towards businesses than to consumers. For this reason, the CPI, which only measures a particular cross section of the market, grows more slowly than M2, and also more slowly than business profits. Statistical Genealogy, or Knowing what is an extraordinary claim
 It is often said in genealogy (or any field of research, really) that “extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence”. Fair enough. But how does one know what is an extraordinary claim? We can extrapolate from our own experience and society, but our ancestors often lived in very different times and circumstances. What might seem extraordinary or strange to us might have been quite common to them and  vice versa .  

 I'm a moderator on the Mathematica.SE site, so I’m aware of the  social network analysis capabilities in Mathematica , even though I’ve never really used them. They, and a  recent post on Stephen Wolfram’s blog  got me thinking about the genealogical equivalent.  

 The big sites like Ancestry.com, Familysearch.org and FindMyPast.co.uk have all collected literally millions of trees and built up profiles of tens of millions of individuals and families. It seems obvious that one could build up  statistical  statements about what was most common historically, and then people could compare their current hypotheses about their own ancestors to these statements to help decide if they are making “extraordinary claims”. I’ll give some examples to show what I mean. Bear in mind that the following are all completely made up, but are the sort of thing I had in mind: 

 
   15% of men and 16% of women born in 18th century England married more than once; only 2% of either men or women married more than twice. (  ok so my great^4 grandmother probably didn't marry five times and those are different Alice Smiths...  ) 
 

 Or: 

 
   94% of people who were not nobility born in Kent between 1650 and 1800 married someone born within twenty miles of them. Less than 1% married someone born more than 50 miles away. (  ok so I can probably rule out that baptism from Lancashire as being for my great^5 grandfather who married and died in Dorset... ) 
 

 Or: 

 
   Only 10% of men born in the 1700s in England who subsequently married did so for the first time after they turned 30, and if their parents married before the age of 25, only 3% married after the age of 30. (  hmm, so my great^5 uncle is probably that guy, not that guy who married eight years later. So his wife is most likely to be this woman not that one... ) 
 

 So my question is:  has anyone done this, even over a restricted field such as a particular century or country?  Surely there is a statistically-minded Mormon over at FamilySearch or wherever who has thought of doing this? While the exceptional cases clearly can still have happened, it would surely help people  formulate  their hypotheses if they had an idea how likely or unlikely certain outcomes might have been. 

  EDIT  

 Lots of good responses in the answers and comments. I agree that the data are very dirty. But I'm an economist and thus used to dealing with messy, poorly measured data. The question is whether the errors in the data are enough to materially skew the kinds of statistical statements I have in mind. I can imagine that there would be some skew away from correct conclusions that happened to be unusual (the thrice-married woman, the 17th century couple born 100 miles apart etc). But for a lot of things, the errors in people’s trees would cancel each other out. I think this is the difference between a statistical approach and an historical approach.

In this model, progress is viewed as steady and cumulative, moving from primitive tools to metallurgy and monumental architecture. 
 By contrast,  ancient Indian texts describe a cyclic model , where civilizations rise and fall repeatedly over vast ages. The period traditionally associated with  Lord Rama and Lord Krishna , spanning tens of thousands of years, is often cited in these texts. Importantly, the cyclic model does  not require literal gods . These figures can be interpreted symbolically, representing civilizations, their societal organization, and technological advancement at different stages. This allows the model to be considered in terms of historical and cultural development rather than purely religious narrative. 
 Yet, when archaeologists study highly advanced ancient structures, such as the  Kailasa Temple at Ellora  or  Dwarka's submerged ruins , these are almost always explained strictly within the linear model, attributed to later humans using relatively primitive technology. Where this seems insufficient, some propose  alien intervention , even though there is  no verifiable evidence . 
 Notably, the cyclic model has  never been seriously considered in peer-reviewed research . Figures like  Dr. Nilesh Nilkanth Oak  propose much earlier dates for the Ramayana and Mahabharata

Motivation and history of Fubini's theorem
 I saw the double integral version of Fubini's theorem on  Wikipedia . 
 
 It was introduced by Guido Fubini in 1907. It states that if a function is Lebesgue integrable on a rectangle  ${\displaystyle X\times Y}$ , then one can evaluate the double integral as an iterated integral y using an iterated integral.
 $${\displaystyle \,\iint \limits _{X\times Y}f(x,y)\,{\text{d}}(x,y)=\int _{X}\left(\int _{Y}f(x,y)\,{\text{d}}y\right){\text{d}}x=\int _{Y}\left(\int _{X}f(x,y)\,{\text{d}}x\right){\text{d}}y.}$$  
 The formula is, in general, not true for the Riemann integral, but it is true if the function is continuous on the rectangle. In multivariable calculus, this weaker result is sometimes also called Fubini's theorem, although it was already known by Leonhard Euler. 
 
 And after looking into it further, I found that there is also a   double series version . 
 
 A related theorem is often called Fubini's theorem for infinite series, although it is due to Alfred Pringsheim this theorem states that if  ${\textstyle \{a_{m,n}\}_{m=1,n=1}^{\infty }}$  is a double-indexed sequence of real numbers, and if  ${\textstyle \displaystyle \sum _{(m,n)\in \mathbb {N} \times \mathbb {N} }a_{m,n}}$  is absolutely convergent, then  ${\displaystyle \sum _{(m,n)\in \mathbb {N} \times \mathbb {N} }a_{m,n}=\sum _{m=1}^{\infty }\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }a_{m,n}=\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\sum _{m=1}^{\infty }a_{m,n}}$  Although Fubini's theorem for infinite series is a special case of the more general Fubini's theorem, it is not necessarily appropriate to characterize the former as being proven by the latter because the properties of measures needed to prove Fubini's theorem proper, in particular subadditivity of measure, may be proven using Fubini's theorem for infinite series.

How frequently is foreign press barred or allowed in war zones?
 (Yes, this is motivated by the question about press access to Gaza, but don't read support, or criticism, for that question in this one.  Merely curiosity about how much we can expect free press access in conflict zones). 
 
 To give some context of my understanding coming into this question: 
 
 During the Vietnam War, the US, consciously or not, experimented with press freedom in a war zone.  This was largely seen to have been a mistake from the US PoV,  whether or not one agreed with war itself .  From burning napalm on a child, to a self-immolating monk, to a spot execution of a bound communist sympathizer, a number of instantly-recognizable photos contributed in driving down US domestic support for the war. 
 
 I kinda recall people stating that that access had been a)  unusual  and b) mismanaged.  With the  unusual  aspect relevant to my question here. 
 
  By Gulf War 1, the US had learned its lesson and the press coverage about press coverage was fascinated by the solution found:   embedded journalists .  Who were vetted, and controlled by, the Pentagon.  So, yes, there was access.  But, no, it wasn't  free  access.  And, if I recall correctly, no one was much surprised or outraged, just a bit cynical about the press freedom quotient to be expected. 
 
  In the Ukraine war, the press does have access to the Ukraine side of things.  But even people highly sympathetic to Ukraine can understand that Ukraine has a vested interest in presenting its plight on the world stage.  Free press access is  of benefit  to Ukraine, which is not doubt a huge part of the reasons it is allowed. 
 
 On the Russian side of things, no, I don't think there is free access to foreign journalists to the occupied regions.  They do conduct  tours , of sorts, mostly with picked Western "journalists" of dubious quality. 
 
 
  India has found it expedient at times to bar foreign press in Kashmir for months at a time.   RSF in 2020 :  "The Kashmir Valley, from which foreign reporters had already been barred for several months"  
 
  Yes, there are plenty of counterinsurgency conflicts - presumably what Gaza is supposed to be at this point - where press is allowed, under various levels of control, by the official government.  But in many cases, the "coverage of the coverage" also points out the reason:  the government wants to appear strong and in control and a press blackout would give the opposite impression.  Keep that in mind when looking at historical access to Gaza - just because it was allowed at one time doesn't mean the same calculation about the cost/benefit applies nowadays, from the Israeli side. 
 
 Yes, at times Israel has allowed foreign press into Gaza, under highly controlled conditions, for example to show tunnels under hospitals.  This is akin to Gulf War 1 embedded reporters and isn't generally seen as free press access. 
 
 
  Guerrillas, rebels and sometimes even terrorists often explicitly covet coverage, consider press access a  tool  in their struggle and therefore allow it.  But, like Ukraine, one should be under no illusion about why this is allowed, regardless of where one's sympathy lies. 
 
 
 
  So, on balance is foreign press access the norm, or the exception, in conflict zones, on the government side?  Especially by democracies, rather than authoritarian regimes.  
  p.s. At the risk of stating the obvious, the press itself will almost always insist on press freedom.  This question  isn't  about what the press thinks, nor whether  public opinion  thinks that the press should be allowed or not.  It is concerned with what is  normative/customary  with regards to foreign press access in war zones.  
 p.p.s. Be cautious about  survivor bias  here.  Merely citing all the conflict coverage you can recall doesn't tell us much about the cases where it wasn't allowed. 
 p.p.p.s.  It was already in the comments, but it seems to have been missed:   while it is motivated by the Gaza situation this question is explicitly  not about Gaza : we already know the foreign press is barred there.
